final_answer: Best answer: the District of South Carolina (4th Circuit) office, with moderate confidence and an important caveat. Reasoning: (1) Under USSG 1B1.3 relevant conduct and 3D1.2(d) grouping, the loss from the false claims in both states is aggregated under 2B1.1 whichever district prosecutes, so the Guidelines range turns on total loss, not on which state the claims were filed in; a single indictment is preferable to two prosecutions because it produces one grouped range and avoids a second sentencing at which a court may run sentences concurrently (5G1.3). Each 1347 count carries a 10-year maximum (20 if serious bodily injury), and 5G1.2(d) allows stacking counts to reach the total punishment if the range exceeds the highest single-count maximum. (2) The circuits differ on how loss is read. The Fourth Circuit, applying Kisor, treats 'loss' in 2B1.1 as ambiguous and defers to the commentary (greater of actual or intended loss; billed amount as prima facie evidence of intended loss in government health-care program cases). The Eleventh Circuit en banc in United States v. Dupree (2023) held that commentary cannot expand a guideline's text absent ambiguity, and later panels questioned intended loss, which favors defendants. Hence, as to conduct sentenced before the November 1, 2024 amendment, the D.S.C. forum is more favorable to the government. (3) Caveat: Amendment 827 (eff. Nov. 1, 2024) moved the 'greater of actual or intended loss' rule into the guideline text itself, which largely eliminates the Dupree/Banks problem for post-amendment sentencing, making the two forums close to equivalent on loss. I did not verify post-amendment Eleventh Circuit case law, and did not independently resolve whether venue lies in one district for both states' claims (each execution of a scheme is arguably a separate offense; 18 U.S.C. 3237(a) continuing-offense venue and Rule 18 may or may not reach both states). If venue does not reach both states' conduct, each office could only charge its own counts, but relevant conduct under 1B1.3 still lets either court count the other state's fraud in loss. Unresolved: facts not given (which state had greater loss, payer identity, where claims were processed), which could change the choice; if the larger share of the loss or the claim processing occurred in Georgia, venue and proof considerations may favor S.D. Ga. This answer rests partly on secondary sources and search summaries, not retrieved primary texts.
